version_note_1_4_0: 1.4.0 adds treaty_layer, the layer of authority above every lever: the Ramsar Convention, the Bonn Convention, the three bilateral migratory bird agreements, the East Asian-Australasian Flyway Partnership, the Paris Agreement and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, each carrying what it obliges, whom it binds, how it reaches this island if it does at all, and what it does not do. Only one of the nine obligations prohibits anything, and the act it prohibits does not happen in this simulation. The Moreton Bay Ramsar record was corrected against the site's own 2023 information sheet and its 2018 boundary description, neither of which anybody here had read: the site is 120,639 ha, it meets all nine criteria, it is Flyway Network Site EAAF013, and its line on this island takes in the western flats and steps around the three townships. ROKAMBA's dates were confirmed and its gap closed. Seven levers that already moved shorebird disturbance or the Amity shoreline now name the instruments they run into.
version_note_1_3_0: 1.3.0 adds off_world, the third register, and it is the first block in this file that is deliberately not part of the island default state. It carries the space law that already binds Australia, cited like everything else here, and separately the shape an instrument would have to take if this island ever answered to an authority above the nation state. The interface leaves it switched off until somebody asks for it, no lever, metric, issue or institution may name anything in it, and tools/ingest/checks-offworld.mjs fails the gate if that one-way rule is ever broken.
version_note_1_2_0: 1.2.0 answers a correction from the owner about who the island's transport operators actually are. It adds a state public transport network layer to the jurisdiction, because the pack had none and the island bus therefore read as a third private operator alongside the two boats when it is a Queensland Government network service run by a contractor. It records that the barge operator and the bus operator share a listed parent. It records the Stradbroke Flyer as a separate family business. And it records, from Translink's own journey planner, that no boat to this island is a Translink service, which turns the cost-of-crossing grievance from an inference into a cited boundary. No lever's who_decides changed: the six levers naming SeaLink are about commercial water services and were correctly attributed.
version_note: 1.1.0 adds two top-level blocks that other files now depend on: citation_rule, which the gate enforces so that every citation in this pack resolves to a registered source, and decision_postures, which src/systems/civic/council.js reads to decide whether a body gets an appetite score at all. Every institution gained a decides_by. Two sentences that overstated what the records below them say were corrected and the correction is recorded beside them rather than quietly made.
island: Minjerribah / North Stradbroke Island, Quandamooka Country, Queensland, Australia
about: The civic machine of Minjerribah as a policy graph. Institutions, the instruments that bind them, the constituencies that react, the metrics that move, and the levers that move them. The design point is that almost nothing here is the player's to decide alone. This island is governed by a council whose seat also covers a mainland suburb, a state government two departments deep, a Commonwealth whose environment law, native title law and grant programs reach it without anybody in Canberra ever coming over, a Registered Native Title Body Corporate holding native title determined by the Federal Court over this island and the waters around it, a jointly managed national park, two commercial boat operators who set their own fares, and a bus operator who sets none because the buses are a Queensland Government network service. A player who wants a thing must usually persuade somebody else to do it, and the first question is always which of those bodies actually holds it.
honesty: No lever here is a promise that a system implements it. This is content, not code.
Where a real plan, budget line or statute exists, it is cited. Where a lever is a modelling construct with no current proposal behind it, status says so and confidence is low.
Every cost is an estimate unless a published figure is cited, and published figures carry the year they were published. Construction costs on an island move fast.
Magnitudes are modelling values on a shared scale. They are not measured elasticities. Nobody has given this project measured elasticities for this island.
who_decides is the most important field in the file. It is deliberately, frequently, not the player.

Every institution carries a tier. Counting bodies makes a long list; counting tiers says how hard a thing is, because a lever that needs the council and the state and the Commonwealth needs three governments to agree and a lever that needs the council needs one.

The Commonwealth is a decider on very few levers and a constraint on many. Adding it to who_decides where it does not hold the decision would be as wrong as leaving it out where it does, so most of its weight in this pack sits in instruments rather than in levers.
Ferry, barge, bus and parking capacity numbers belong in data/transport.json, not here. This pack references them and does not restate them.
Nothing cultural is generated here. QYAC appears as a civic and corporate actor with sourced public functions and nothing more.

One block in this file is not about the island as it is. off_world is the third register, it is off in the interface until somebody turns it on, and while it is off nothing on any screen differs by a number. Everything outside that block is a known claim with a citation. Inside it, every record says which of the three registers it is in, and the speculative ones say what they were lifted from and what would settle them.

confidence_scale.high: A named public source states this directly, or it is a matter of public record such as a statute or a determination.
confidence_scale.medium: A credible public source supports it but the figure, date or scope may have moved, or it is inferred from two sources that agree.
confidence_scale.low: Plausible and useful for the simulation, but not verified. Do not show it to a player as fact.

field_guide.institutions[].tier: commonwealth | state | local | native_title | joint | private | none. Which order of government or kind of body it is. A lever's difficulty is derived from how many distinct tiers appear in its who_decides, which is a different and more useful number than how many bodies appear.
field_guide.levers[].id: stable slug, safe as a key
field_guide.levers[].who_decides: one or more institution ids from this file's institutions list. The decision maker, not the funder and not the lobbyist.
field_guide.levers[].player_role: player_decides | player_funds | player_advocates | player_observes. The honest answer to 'can I just do this'.
field_guide.levers[].status: in_place | funded | proposed | under_study | modelled_option | contested. modelled_option means nobody has actually proposed it and this pack invented the framing, not the facts.
field_guide.levers[].cost_aud: capital is a one-off in A$; recurring_per_year is ongoing in A$; basis says where the number came from.
field_guide.levers[].lead_time_months: from decision to the effect starting to appear, not to ribbon cutting.
field_guide.levers[].effects[]: {target, magnitude, delay_months, confidence}. target is a metric id from this file's metrics list.
field_guide.levers[].effects[].magnitude: signed, -1 to +1, as a fraction of that metric's plausible full swing on this island. +0.1 is a real but modest shift. +0.6 is transformative. Sign is in the metric's own units, so a positive magnitude on a metric whose direction is 'lower_is_better' is a worsening.
field_guide.levers[].side_effects[]: second-order consequences a player should be able to discover rather than be told. Same shape as effects plus a description.
field_guide.levers[].who_supports / who_opposes: interest_group ids. Empty is allowed and means genuinely nobody organised cares much.
field_guide.interest_groups[].size: share of the island's civic weight, 0 to 1, across residents plus the non-resident groups that show up to consultation. The set does not sum to 1 because people belong to several groups at once and because visitors are not residents.
field_guide.interest_groups[].base_mood: -1 furious to +1 delighted, at the pack's baseline state with no levers pulled.
field_guide.metrics[].baseline: the value the simulation should start from. index means a 0 to 1 modelling index with no published measurement behind it.
field_guide.metrics[].direction: higher_is_better | lower_is_better | context. context means the value is neither good nor bad on its own.

source_registry.repo-direction: docs/DIRECTION.md in this repository. Item 6 sets the three registers and requires every claim to name the test that would settle it; item 8 lists the generic decision shapes; and the standing constraint at the end of it records why there is no conflict anywhere in this build.
source_registry.repo-lore: data/lore.json in this repository, which holds the cultural prohibitions the gate reads out of the pack and runs over every file, this block included.
source_registry.repo-ingest: docs/INGEST.md in this repository, which sets the record envelope, the status classifier and the rule that a proposal stays proposed.
source_registry.ow-unoosa-treaties: The five United Nations treaties on outer space, and the status tables for them that the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs compiles and publishes annually at unoosa.org. The status table, rather than any single page, is where a current count of parties lives, which is why no record in this pack states one.
source_registry.ow-cospar-policy: The COSPAR Policy on Planetary Protection, adopted and maintained by the Committee on Space Research and published by COSPAR. Read for its published structure of mission categories rather than line by line, which is why no category's requirements are stated in this pack.
source_registry.ow-antarctic-treaty: The Antarctic Treaty, done at Washington on 1 December 1959 and in force from 23 June 1961. Text and consultative meeting records published by the Antarctic Treaty Secretariat at ats.aq.
source_registry.ow-unclos-text: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Part XI and Article 136. Text published by the United Nations and by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea at itlos.org.
source_registry.ow-isa-about: The International Seabed Authority, established under Part XI of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and operating from 1994. Its instruments and the state of its exploitation regulations are published at isa.org.jm and were not read line by line for this pack.
source_registry.brief: Task brief supplied by the author, not independently verified
source_registry.rcc-chas-strategy: Redland City Council Coastal Hazard Adaptation Strategy, 48 pages. Read through tools/ingest/lane-document.mjs from the copy registered in data/_provenance.json.documents as rcc-chas-strategy, sha256 197d6cf06ea11325.

citation_rule.about: Every citation field in this pack holds exactly one key of source_registry above. tools/ingest/checks-citations.mjs resolves all of them on every gate run and fails blocking on any that names nothing, because a citation that resolves to nothing reads as cited, renders as cited, and is worse than an admitted gap. A bare URL pasted into a record fails the same check: register it and cite the id, so that one edit moves every record resting on it.
citation_rule.fields: Any field named source, or ending in _source: second_source, third_source, quote_source, money_source, capacity_source, commonwealth_source.

uncited.general knowledge: Not a citation. It is the declaration that this record has no published source at all: a modelling index somebody chose so the simulation had a number, not a measurement anybody took. Every record carrying it sits at low confidence and says so.

citation_rule.why_the_limit: A metric baseline is a modelling parameter and docs/INGEST.md is explicit that demanding a quotation for a number nobody published is how invented quotations get into packs. An institution, an instrument, a lever, a jurisdiction layer or a matter of national environmental significance is a claim about who holds power over a real island, and none of those may say general knowledge. The gate enforces the difference rather than trusting it.

jurisdiction.summary: Three townships, one council division shared with a mainland suburb, roughly half the island in a jointly managed national park, native title determined in 2011 under Commonwealth law over 24,903 hectares onshore and 29,505 offshore, an internationally listed wetland that takes in this island and that Commonwealth environment law protects, and every road on and off the island in somebody else's hands.
jurisdiction.summary_note: Every figure in that sentence is in a record below and none of it is rounded up. The native title figures are the determination's own, 2,264 hectares exclusive possession and 22,639 non-exclusive onshore, and a determination area is not the same thing as an island: this pack has not mapped the determination against the island's cadastre and so it does not say that the whole island is inside it. Nor does it hold the Commonwealth's Ramsar boundary description, so it says the wetland takes in the island and stops there. The earlier version of this sentence said native title was determined over the whole island and that half the island was inside the wetland. Neither was in any record in this pack, and anybody who owns a block in Dunwich would have known the first one was wrong.

tiers.note: Four orders of authority reach this island, plus the bodies that are not government at all. A lever's difficulty is how many of these have to agree, not how many names are on it. The eighth entry, international, is listed first and is not one of them: nobody at it decides anything here, holds a lever, answers a submission or stands for election, and a lever cannot be made easier by getting it to agree. It is in the order so that an instrument at that level is filed under a heading rather than under none. What sits there is in treaty_layer.
tiers.governments_note: Three of the eight tiers are orders of government in the ordinary sense, and counting how many of those three a lever needs is the honest measure of how hard it is. The other five are an international obligation nobody here can move, a native title body corporate, a joint arrangement, private parties and nobody, and each is hard in its own way rather than in that way.

layers.covers: National environment law over the Ramsar wetland that takes in the island's western flats and its perched lakes, the listed threatened and migratory species on them, cetaceans in Commonwealth waters, the Native Title Act under which the 2011 determination was made and the ILUAs registered, telecommunications and postal service obligations, aviation safety and the airspace, biosecurity at the national border, and grant programs that mostly arrive through the state or the council rather than directly.
layers.why_it_matters: Nobody from the Commonwealth sits in a room on this island, and it still holds a veto over the mainland ferry terminal the island depends on. That is what a fourth tier looks like from here.

layers.covers: Roads in the townships, waste, water and wastewater through Redland Water, parks and foreshore, local laws including dogs and camping on council land, the planning scheme, rates.
One councillor. Division 2 covers Cleveland on the mainland and North Stradbroke Island together, so the island's representative also answers to a mainland suburb with far more voters.
layers.why_it_matters: This single fact shapes every island grievance about being outvoted.

layers.covers: The statute that ended mining, the transition funding, national park, marine park, coastal management, planning appeals, health, schools, police, public transport contracts.

Determined native title over Minjerribah since 4 July 2011, the ILUAs that set how those rights are exercised, joint management of the national park, and the island's camping and vehicle access business.
Naree Budjong Djara National Park and the Minjerribah Recreation Area, jointly managed by QYAC and QPWS under an Indigenous Management Agreement.

layers.layer: Private operators on a public function
layers.covers: The vehicle barge and a passenger service between Cleveland and Dunwich. Commercial pricing, commercial timetable, no ballot, no resident quota published. Translink carries both water crossings in its journey planner and links their fares out as non-Translink, so the state prints the times and the operator sets the price.
layers.why_it_matters: This is the layer with no vote in it at all. On the island's roads a resident is inside a state network with a 50 cent fare; on the water between the island and their work they are a customer.

layers.covers: Translink, the Queensland Government's public transport brand and network for South East Queensland, administered by the Department of Transport and Main Roads. It plans, contracts, timetables and prices island bus routes 880 and 881: the fares are the Queensland flat network fares of 50 cents single, A$1 daily and A$5 weekly, with no go card and a paper ticket instead, and the 1 December 2025 service increase was announced by Translink as part of the Queensland Government's commitment to capacity and connectivity on the island. From that date the island's bus information moved from the qconnect brand to Translink.
layers.why_it_matters: The pack used to have no layer for this at all, so the island bus read as a third private operator alongside the two boats. It is not. It is the one piece of the island's transport that already sits inside a public network with a public fare, and it is the thing the cost-of-crossing levers are asking for on the water.

decision_postures.about: How a body arrives at a decision, which is not the same question as what it decides. Until this block existed the board printed one number for every body on it, a 0 to 100 appetite, including on the federal environment department, directly above a line saying the minister decides against a statutory test and not against how much the island wants it. Both cannot be true. A meter that says wanting it more helps is a claim about the decision, so the bodies where that is false do not get one.
decision_postures.field: institutions[].decides_by. src/systems/civic/council.js reads it, sets no appetite where meter is false, and scores those decisions without the public case, the petitions, the deputations or your standing, because none of those is an input to them.

weighs_it_up.label: Appetite right now
weighs_it_up.what_moves_it: Budget headroom, the mood of the constituency it answers to, and how many files you already have open with it. Asking one body for five things at once costs you.
weighs_it_up.note: A body with money, a constituency and a choice. Here, wanting it more genuinely does help.

commercial.label: Commercial appetite
commercial.what_moves_it: Whether it pays, and whether it pays this year.
commercial.note: A private operator on a public function. It can be asked, it cannot be directed, and the question it asks itself is not the one you are asking.

volunteer_capacity.label: Whether anybody is left to do it
volunteer_capacity.what_moves_it: How the volunteers are feeling and how ready the island is. Some things here happen because people do them, or do not happen because nobody is left to.
volunteer_capacity.note: Not a chamber and not a budget. A roster.

statutory_test.label: What it decides against
statutory_test.what_moves_it: Nothing on this island. The test is in the Act. The file either meets it or it does not, and the strength of local feeling is not one of the matters the decision maker may take into account.
statutory_test.instead: So this board does not print an appetite for this body. What it prints is the test, the clock, and whether your file is complete, because completeness is the only part of it you hold.

competitive_round.label: How the round works
competitive_round.what_moves_it: Every other application in Australia that year, which this twin does not model and will not guess at. Being deserving is not the variable and neither is being liked.
competitive_round.instead: So this board does not print an appetite for this body either. A round does not remember you, and next year's round is a fresh one.

not_modelled.label: Not modelled
not_modelled.what_moves_it: This twin does not simulate this body's decisions at all. It models the referral, the documented constraint and the wait, and then it stops.
not_modelled.instead: You can record your own assumption to keep playing, and everything downstream stays labelled as resting on it rather than on anybody's position.

decision_postures.gap: The postures are a modelling judgement about how these bodies decide, not a published classification. What is cited is the machinery each one names: the section 75 clock, the Division 2 boundary, the funding program. Nobody has been asked whether they recognise the label.

institutions.label: Redland City Council
institutions.role: Roads, parks, foreshore, waste, water and wastewater, planning scheme, local laws, rates. The island is one part of a city whose population is overwhelmingly on the mainland.

institutions.label: Division 2 councillor
institutions.role: The island's single voice in the council chamber, in a division that also covers Cleveland on the mainland.
institutions.note: The pack deliberately does not name the sitting councillor. Names change; the structure does not.

institutions.label: Redland Water
institutions.role: Reticulated water and the sewerage network in the townships, and the Point Lookout wastewater treatment plant.

institutions.label: Seqwater
institutions.role: Bulk water for the island townships, drawn from bores and treated at small local plants. The island is not on the South East Queensland Water Grid.

institutions.label: Queensland Government
institutions.role: The statute that ended mining, the transition funding, the national park, coastal and marine management, planning appeals, health, schools, police, public transport contracts.

institutions.label: Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation
institutions.role: Administers Minjerribah Futures and holds the parks and environment functions. The department has been renamed and restructured more than once during the transition, which the audit office found disrupted the program.

institutions.label: Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service
institutions.role: Joint manager of Naree Budjong Djara National Park and the Minjerribah Recreation Area with QYAC.

institutions.label: Joint management, QYAC and QPWS
institutions.role: Indigenous Joint Management Areas run under an Indigenous Management Agreement. Fire, pests, weeds, cultural heritage, assets and visitor management on park.
institutions.note: For any lever on park, this is the decision maker, not the council and not the player.

institutions.label: Quandamooka Yoolooburrabee Aboriginal Corporation
institutions.role: Holds and manages the native title rights and interests of the Quandamooka People recognised on 4 July 2011. Joint manager of the national park. Operator of Minjerribah Camping. Around 550 members, the largest membership of any prescribed body corporate in Australia.
institutions.capacity_note: The Queensland Audit Office found QYAC was assigned multiple complex construction projects at once, with fewer than 100 staff, without an adequate capacity assessment. Capacity is a real constraint in this simulation, not a slur.

institutions.label: Minjerribah Camping
institutions.role: Runs the island's camping grounds and issues the vehicle access permits for the Minjerribah Recreation Area, including Main Beach and Flinders Beach.

institutions.label: Translink, Department of Transport and Main Roads
institutions.role: Translink is the Queensland Government's public transport brand and network for South East Queensland, administered by the Department of Transport and Main Roads. On this island it plans, contracts, timetables and prices bus routes 880 and 881: the fares are Queensland's flat network fares of 50 cents single, A$1 daily and A$5 weekly, published by Translink, with no go card and a separate paper ticket. It announced the 1 December 2025 service increase as part of the Queensland Government's commitment to improving capacity and connectivity on the island, and says it developed the changes with the local operator, which is a consultation and not a decision.
institutions.boundary: The network stops at the water. Translink carries both walk-on crossings and the vehicle barge in its journey planner and links every one of their fares out as non-Translink, so no boat to this island is a Translink service and no boat fare is Translink's to set.
institutions.moved_here: Until 1 December 2025 the island's bus information sat under the qconnect brand. The Queensland Government's own qconnect page for North Stradbroke Island now says all information on North Stradbroke Island services can be found on the Translink website.
institutions.note: The brand is styled Translink by its own publisher, whose page title reads North Stradbroke Island fares and tickets | Translink. TransLink with a capital L is the older styling and is still used by operators and in reporting. This pack uses Translink.

institutions.label: Transit Systems QLD
institutions.role: Runs island bus routes 880 between Dunwich and Point Lookout and 881 between One Mile, Dunwich and Amity Point. It runs them, it does not price them and it does not publish their timetable on its own account: those belong to Translink. Its own commercial work here is charter, school transfers and excursions, which sit outside the contract.
institutions.trading_names: Trades on the island as the North Stradbroke Island Bus Service and is still widely called Stradbroke Island Buses. Transit Systems acquired the business in December 2022 and renamed it Transit Systems QLD in early 2023.
institutions.name_conflict: Translink's own 1 December 2025 release names the local operator Bay Island Transit Systems, which is the name this pack carried until now. The operator's own site, the Queensland Government's page and the Transit Systems operations page all say Transit Systems or Transit Systems QLD. The two have not been reconciled from any public source and both are recorded rather than one being picked.
institutions.owner_group: A Kelsian Group company, on its own statement. Kelsian Group is the renamed SeaLink Travel Group, so the island's bus operator and the island's barge operator answer to one listed parent: contracted on the road, commercial on the water. A player pressing the operator is pressing one group wearing two hats, and the hat decides whether the answer is a commercial no or a referral to the state.

institutions.label: Economic Development Queensland
institutions.role: Administers the Toondah Harbour Priority Development Area on the mainland side, which contains the vehicle ferry terminal the island depends on.

institutions.label: SeaLink South East Queensland
institutions.role: Vehicle barge and passenger service, Cleveland to Dunwich. Trading as Stradbroke Ferries Pty Ltd. Commercial: it sets its own fares and its own timetable, and no contract obliges it to run anything.
institutions.not_a_network_service: Translink carries this crossing in its journey planner as Stradbroke Island Dunwich SeaLink and links the fare out as non-Translink. So the 50 cent fare that applies on the island's buses does not apply to the boat that gets people to them, and that is the sourced shape of the cost-of-crossing grievance rather than an inference.
institutions.owner_group: A Kelsian Group company, the same parent as the island's bus operator. SeaLink Travel Group bought Transit Systems in a sale completed January 2020 and renamed itself Kelsian Group in November 2021; Transit Systems acquired the island bus service in December 2022. Two levers aimed at two operators may be aimed at one company.

institutions.label: Stradbroke Flyer Gold Cat
institutions.role: Passenger water taxi, Cleveland to One Mile at Dunwich. A second and separate operator on the same crossing, landing about a kilometre north of where SeaLink lands. Its own terminal on Emmett Drive at Cleveland, its own jetty at One Mile, its own fleet, its own fares and its own ticketing.
institutions.ownership: Family owned and operated, in one family since 1986, with three generations in the business on the operator's own account. It is not owned by SeaLink, Transit Systems, Kelsian or Translink and it is not a subsidiary of any of them, and no source found in this pass links it to any of them.
institutions.not_a_network_service: Translink carries it as Stradbroke Island One Mile Flyer, under its own operator name, and links the fare out as non-Translink.
institutions.handling_rule: This is a small family business in a public twin of the island it works. Nothing in this project may render, group, badge, total or price it as SeaLink's, and nothing may give it a SeaLink vessel or a SeaLink capacity. Getting that wrong is worse than a data bug.

institutions.label: Sibelco Australia
institutions.role: Ran the island's sand mining to its close and signed a rehabilitation agreement in December 2019 committing to work with QYAC on restoring and surrendering former mining land.

institutions.label: Private landowners
institutions.role: At Amity Point, owners of land behind the central reach of the foreshore carry the construction and maintenance cost of works that protect their own property.

institutions.label: Australian Government
institutions.role: The Commonwealth. It makes the law under which native title over this island was determined and the island's land use agreements were registered, it protects the Ramsar wetland and the listed species on it under national environment law, it sets telecommunications, postal and aviation obligations, it holds biosecurity at the national border, and it pays for things here through programs. It has no office on the island and no officer who lives here.
institutions.seats_on_island: None. The island sits in a federal electorate whose voters are overwhelmingly on the mainland, which is the same shape of problem as Division 2 one tier down.
institutions.money_note: Almost no Commonwealth money reaches this island as a cheque from Canberra. Financial assistance grants are paid to Queensland and passed to the council on the state grants commission's recommendation, disaster funding is jointly funded and administered by the Queensland Reconstruction Authority, and the transition program that reshaped this island is a state program. The Commonwealth is more often the condition on a decision than the maker of one.

institutions.label: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
institutions.role: Administers the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. A person proposing an action likely to have a significant impact on a matter of national environmental significance refers it, and the environment minister decides whether it is a controlled action and, if it is, whether to approve it and on what conditions. This is the one Commonwealth decision that has already landed on this island's front door.
institutions.note: The pack deliberately does not name the sitting minister. Ministers and department names change; the decision does not. The department has been renamed more than once, which is why the Act is cited rather than the letterhead.
institutions.capacity_note: The referral decision under section 75 runs to a statutory clock of twenty business days. Everything after it does not: a controlled action goes to an assessment that is measured in seasons, and the Toondah referral sat with the Commonwealth from 2018 to 2024.

institutions.label: No formal decision maker
institutions.role: Some things on this island happen because volunteers do them, or do not happen because nobody is left to. Used where a lever has no institutional owner.
institutions.note: The Amity Point Progress Association has wound up, so Amity Point has no local progress association to consult.

instruments.label: North Stradbroke Island Protection and Sustainability Act 2011
instruments.what_it_does: Set the framework for phasing out sand mining on the island. Amended in 2016 to bring the end date back to the end of 2019.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the reason the island has an economy in transition rather than a mine.

instruments.label: Quandamooka People #1 and #2 determination
instruments.what_it_does: Recognised native title over 54,408 hectares: 2,264 hectares exclusive possession, 22,639 hectares onshore non-exclusive, 29,505 hectares offshore non-exclusive. Delaney on behalf of the Quandamooka People v State of Queensland [2011] FCA 741.

instruments.label: The Quandamooka Indigenous Land Use Agreements
instruments.what_it_does: Two agreements setting how native title rights and interests are exercised on the ground, including the joint management arrangements. The Quandamooka and State of Queensland ILUA was registered by the National Native Title Tribunal on 8 December 2011.
instruments.gap: The full text and the specific schedules that govern camping, tourism and land dealings were not read for this pack.

instruments.label: Naree Budjong Djara management plan
instruments.what_it_does: Sets how QYAC and QPWS jointly manage the national park and the visitor experience within it. Naree Budjong Djara means My Mother Earth.

instruments.label: North Stradbroke Island Economic Transition Strategy
instruments.what_it_does: The original transition package, 23 projects, designed to move the island off sand mining.

instruments.label: Minjerribah Futures
instruments.what_it_does: The successor program to the transition strategy. Approved funding rose from an initial $20 million to $39.4 million as at 30 April 2024, of which $30.6 million had been spent. $8.74 million went directly to QYAC between July 2016 and December 2021.
instruments.audit_findings: The strategy assumed $36.6 million in private investment that never arrived, which forced the state to raise its own contribution. Governance was found to be complex and inconsistent, with inadequate community oversight.

instruments.label: Gumpi (Dunwich) Master Plan
instruments.what_it_does: Sets future residential, commercial, community, environmental and industrial land uses at Dunwich, infrastructure upgrades and the gateway role. A temporary local planning instrument covered 25 land parcels across Gumpi, Pulan Pulan and Mulumba.
instruments.gap: Whether the master plan has been given effect in the current Redland City Plan was not confirmed.

instruments.label: Amity Point Shoreline Erosion Management Plan
instruments.what_it_does: A 20 year plan splitting the Amity Point foreshore into three reaches. Northern reach: surveys and coastal process studies. Central reach: formalising and maintaining the rock flow slide barrier. Southern reach: a buried seawall and sand nourishment.

instruments.label: Coastal Hazard Adaptation Strategy
instruments.what_it_does: A 20 to 100 year plan for erosion, sea level rise and storm tide across the whole city coastline. The 2016 current hazards phase identified Amity Point as the only area at high risk of coastal erosion.

instruments.label: Declared erosion prone area
instruments.what_it_does: Amity Point is a declared erosion prone area under the Coastal Protection and Management Act 1995, which constrains what can be built and where.

instruments.label: Quandamooka water reserves
instruments.what_it_does: Established two water reserves totalling 61,190 megalitres for the Quandamooka People, split evenly between environmental and cultural use and economic use and land rehabilitation, from water previously allocated to sand mining.

instruments.label: Sibelco rehabilitation agreement
instruments.what_it_does: Commits Sibelco to work with QYAC on rehabilitating and surrendering former mining land on the island.

instruments.label: Toondah Harbour Priority Development Area
instruments.what_it_does: The mainland end of the island's vehicle ferry link, declared a Priority Development Area in 2013. The private development partner withdrew its federal application in April 2024, days after the federal environment minister announced a proposed refusal. As reported in April 2026, the Priority Development Area remains in place but has no private sector partner and the redevelopment pathway is unclear.
instruments.why_it_matters: The island's front door on the mainland has no development partner and no settled plan. Every access lever runs through this uncertainty. The withdrawn proposal had included a new ferry terminal, so the terminal upgrade went with it.

instruments.label: Redland Local Housing Action Plan
instruments.what_it_does: Council's housing actions, which record that businesses on the island struggle to recruit because there is nowhere for workers to live, and that the island housing co-operative had no vacancies across its portfolio.
instruments.gap: The plan PDF returned 403 to this agent and was read only through search result extracts. Figures should be checked against the document itself.

instruments.label: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Part 3, the matters of national environmental significance. Section 16 for a declared Ramsar wetland, section 18 for a listed threatened species or ecological community, section 20 for a listed migratory species, section 23 for a Commonwealth marine area. Part 7 is the referral, section 75 is the decision on whether an action is a controlled action, and Part 9 is the approval.
instruments.what_it_does: Makes it an offence to take an action that has, will have or is likely to have a significant impact on one of the matters of national environmental significance without the environment minister's approval. The proponent refers the action, the minister has twenty business days to decide whether it is a controlled action, and a controlled action is then assessed and approved, approved with conditions, or refused.
instruments.why_it_matters: This island carries at least four of those matters at once, and the twin already simulates two of them without ever saying whose law they belong to: the western sand flats where the eastern curlew and the bar-tailed godwit roost, and the koala habitat the planning overlay argues about. The Act does not manage the island. It sits over anybody who wants to do something to it.
instruments.gap: The section numbers are as the Act stands on the public consolidations cited. No legal advice was taken and no referral for anything on this island was read.

instruments.label: Moreton Bay Ramsar site
instruments.criteria_met: All nine. The Ramsar Information Sheet published on 1 December 2023 records the site as meeting every criterion for designation as a Wetland of International Importance.
instruments.the_island_in_the_line: The 2018 boundary description delineates the site into four areas, and Area 4 is Stradbroke Islands and Southern Bay. On Minjerribah the site takes in the western intertidal by way of fish habitat area FHA-017, named Myora to Amity Banks, whose separate section runs along the western boundary of the island, together with the landward boundaries of the marine park zones behind it; Myora, being Myora Conservation Park; and two remnant regional ecosystem patches in the south. It excludes freehold unless otherwise noted, and it excludes four named exclusion areas: the Dunwich Ferry Exclusion Area, the Point Lookout Exclusion Area, the Amity Point Exclusion Area and the Southern Exclusion Areas. So the international line on this island runs around the townships and takes in the flats the birds feed on.
instruments.lgas_intersecting: Five local government areas intersect the site. Redland City Council is one of them.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: EPBC Act section 16, which is what turns an international listing into an Australian offence.
instruments.what_it_does: Listed under the Ramsar Convention on 22 October 1993, covering over 120,000 hectares of Moreton Bay and taking in North Stradbroke Island. Australia's obligation is to maintain the site's ecological character and to report any change in it.
instruments.quote: The Ramsar site is home to nationally threatened plant species that are wetland dependent, such as the endangered swamp daisy, Olearia hygrophila, which is only found on North Stradbroke Island.
instruments.why_it_matters: This island is inside an internationally listed wetland, and the shape of that is more interesting than the fact of it: the line takes in the sand flats the shorebirds feed on and steps around the three townships. The site regularly supports more than 50,000 waterbirds and at least 28 migratory shorebird species, and it holds about 9 per cent of the whole flyway population of the eastern curlew. The listing is also the reason the mainland ferry terminal proposal failed: the minister's proposed refusal turned on removing 58.7 hectares from the Ramsar site.
instruments.gap: Corrected 14 August 2026. The earlier version of this record said the boundary description had not been read and that this pack could not say which parts of the island are inside the line. It has now been read and the record says what it names. What is still not resolved is where the exclusion areas fall on the ground: they are defined by cadastral lot and marine park zone rather than by coordinates, this project has no cadastre, and so the twin does not state which side of the line any individual roost sits on. The Queensland fact sheet still cited here is dated 2013 and its figures are as at that date; the area and the criteria above come from the 2023 Ramsar Information Sheet.

instruments.label: Japan and Australia Migratory Bird Agreement
instruments.what_it_does: Signed 6 February 1974 and in force from 30 April 1981. Commits both countries to cooperate on conserving the migratory birds that move between them, and lists those species in an annex.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: A bird on the annex is a listed migratory species under the EPBC Act, so section 20 applies to any action likely to have a significant impact on it.
instruments.why_it_matters: The birds on the flats off Dunwich and Amity Point are on that annex. A treaty signed in Tokyo is the reason a dog off its lead at a high-tide roost is a national matter and not only a local one.
instruments.obliges: Protection and conservation of migratory birds and their important habitats, protection from take or trade except in limited circumstances, the exchange of information, and building cooperative relationships. Not a prohibition on disturbing a roost.

instruments.label: China and Australia Migratory Bird Agreement
instruments.parties: Australia and the People's Republic of China
instruments.what_it_does: Signed 20 October 1986 and in force from 1 September 1988. The same shape as JAMBA: cooperation on the conservation of birds that migrate between the two countries, with the species named in an annex.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: EPBC Act section 20, through the listing of annex species as listed migratory species.
instruments.why_it_matters: The Yellow Sea staging grounds these birds depend on are the pressure the shorebird model already names as beyond any island lever. This is the instrument through which that pressure is anybody's business at all.
instruments.obliges: The same four things as JAMBA: protection and conservation of the birds and their important habitats, protection from take or trade except in limited circumstances, the exchange of information, and building cooperative relationships.

instruments.label: Republic of Korea and Australia Migratory Bird Agreement
instruments.parties: Australia and the Republic of Korea
instruments.what_it_does: The third of the three bilateral migratory bird agreements, with the same structure and the same annex mechanism. Signed at Canberra on 6 December 2006 and in force from 13 July 2007. Like the other two it provides for the protection and conservation of migratory birds and their important habitats, protection from take or trade except in limited circumstances, the exchange of information, and building cooperative relationships.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: EPBC Act section 20.
instruments.why_it_matters: Three treaties, four countries, and a consultative meeting every two years, all of it reaching a sand flat you can walk onto from a caravan park.
instruments.gap: The Australian Treaty Series text was not read for this pack. The dates come from the treaty series entry that the administering department links to, and what the agreement obliges is that department's own summary of all three.

instruments.label: Australian Whale Sanctuary
instruments.the_part_that_bites: EPBC Act section 225, with the offences in Part 13 Division 3.
instruments.what_it_does: Establishes a sanctuary covering the Commonwealth marine area, which begins beyond the three nautical mile limit of state coastal waters and runs out to the edge of the exclusive economic zone. Inside it, killing, injuring, taking, harassing, chasing or herding a cetacean is an offence without a permit.
instruments.why_it_matters: The humpbacks the twin puts past Point Lookout between June and October swim across a jurisdictional line nobody can see. Inshore of it Queensland's rules apply; outside it the Commonwealth's do. It is the clearest example on this island of authority defined by a distance from a baseline rather than by a fence.
instruments.gap: Where exactly the three nautical mile line falls off Point Lookout was not established for this pack, and no approach distance for whale watching is stated here. Queensland sets those in state waters and this pack does not restate them.

instruments.label: The Offshore Constitutional Settlement
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Coastal Waters (State Powers) Act 1980 and Coastal Waters (State Title) Act 1980, in force from 1982 and 1983.
instruments.what_it_does: Divides authority over the sea between the Commonwealth and the states. The states hold powers and title in coastal waters out to three nautical miles from the territorial sea baseline. Beyond that is the Commonwealth marine area.
instruments.why_it_matters: Every marine argument on this island, the marine park, the fisheries closures, the whale approaches, sits on one side of that line or the other, and the pack had no record of where the line is or who drew it.

instruments.label: Native Title Act 1993
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Section 223 defines native title, section 225 is what a determination determines, sections 56 and 57 require the Federal Court to determine a prescribed body corporate to hold or manage the rights, Part 2 Division 3 Subdivision C is the area agreement, and section 199A is the Register of Indigenous Land Use Agreements the Native Title Registrar keeps.
instruments.what_it_does: The Commonwealth law under which the Quandamooka determinations of 4 July 2011 were made, under which QYAC exists as a registered native title body corporate, and under which the island's land use agreements were registered.
instruments.why_it_matters: Fourteen levers in this pack name QYAC as a decision maker and none of them named the law that makes that so. QYAC's standing here is not a courtesy and not a consultation arrangement. It is a Commonwealth statute and a Federal Court determination.
instruments.note: This record names the machinery and nothing else. It records no view of QYAC's, describes no content of any agreement, and the two ILUAs remain unread. See the existing instrument iluas-2011 and docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md B16.

instruments.label: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act 1984
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Section 9 for an emergency declaration and section 10 for other declarations, both made by the Commonwealth minister on application by or on behalf of Aboriginal people, where the minister is satisfied an area is a significant Aboriginal area under threat of injury or desecration.
instruments.what_it_does: Gives a Commonwealth minister the power to declare protection for an area or an object, which can override a state approval.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is recorded here as a mechanism that exists and can be invoked, because a governance model of an Australian place that leaves it out is incomplete. That is the whole of its presence in this project.
instruments.handling_rule: BLOCKING. This project models no application under this Act, no declaration, no area, no site and no threat, and it holds no location. Nothing about it is a lever, a mechanic, an outcome or an event. Naming the Act is a fact about Australian law. Anything beyond naming it would be this project speculating about Quandamooka cultural heritage, which data/lore.json forbids and which is QYAC's alone. Do not model it.

instruments.label: The statutory infrastructure provider regime
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Part 19 of the Telecommunications Act 1997, in force from 1 July 2020.
instruments.what_it_does: Makes NBN Co the default statutory infrastructure provider for Australia, and obliges the provider for an area, on request from a retail service provider, to connect premises and supply a wholesale service capable of at least 25 megabits per second down and 5 up, over fixed line where that is reasonable and over fixed wireless or satellite where it is not.
instruments.why_it_matters: The obligation is to connect a premises on request. It is not an obligation to cover a road, a beach or a headland, which is why the twin's telecoms model can carry dead spots on an island where every house can get a service.
instruments.gap: Which technology serves each township on Minjerribah was not established for this pack. No claim is made about what any island address can actually get.

instruments.label: Australia Post community service obligations
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Section 27 of the Australian Postal Corporation Act 1989.
instruments.what_it_does: Requires Australia Post to supply a letter service, to make it reasonably accessible to all people in Australia on an equitable basis wherever they live, to meet performance standards that reasonably meet the community's social, industrial and commercial needs, and to charge a single uniform rate for a standard letter anywhere in Australia.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the reason a letter to a house at Amity Point costs what a letter across a Brisbane suburb costs, on an island where everything else arrives by barge at a freight rate. One of the very few things here that is deliberately not priced by distance.
instruments.gap: Nothing here states what mail service the island actually receives, how often, or through which outlet. The obligation is on the record; the local arrangement is not.

instruments.label: Aviation safety regulation, and an uncertified strip
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The Civil Aviation Act 1988 and the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations. Part 139 of those regulations sets the standards for certified aerodromes, and it does not apply to one that is not certified.
instruments.what_it_does: The Commonwealth regulates the aircraft, the pilots and the airspace over this island completely. It does not regulate the island's airstrip as an aerodrome, because the strip is not certified. For an uncertified aircraft landing area the operator and the pilot in command decide whether it is fit to use.
instruments.quote_note: The category code published against Dunwich in the En Route Supplement Australia entry, which is the Commonwealth aeronautical publication. The same entry gives runway 15/33, unrated, grass, 800 m, slope 1.5 per cent, elevation 250 ft, CTAF 126.7, no fuel available, full NOTAM service not available, and this under additional information: animal hazard, kangaroo, exists on runway at all times.
instruments.why_it_matters: The island's third door, the one that turns a two hour medical transfer into twenty minutes, is a grass strip with kangaroos on it that no Commonwealth aerodrome standard binds. The airspace above it is regulated to the metre. That gap is the honest shape of Commonwealth authority in a small place.
instruments.gap: The ERSA page was read through a public mirror of the Commonwealth publication rather than from Airservices Australia directly, and the page carries the date 9 July 2026. Aerodrome data changes on a cycle. Read the current ERSA before relying on any figure here. The runway surface differs from the description in data/transport.json, which says gravel and topsoil from the airfield's own guidelines; both are recorded and neither is corrected here.

instruments.label: Commonwealth financial assistance grants to local government
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The Local Government (Financial Assistance) Act 1995, and the national principles made under it.
instruments.what_it_does: The Commonwealth pays untied grants to the states in two components, general purpose and local roads. The states pass them to councils on the recommendation of a state local government grants commission, in Queensland the Queensland Local Government Grants Commission. Once they reach a council the money is untied and the council decides what it is for.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the honest answer to where federal money on this island comes from. It arrives as part of a council budget, allocated by a Queensland commission, and by the time it is spent on a road at Point Lookout nothing about it says Commonwealth. A player looking for a federal lever will not find one here, and that absence is itself the fact.
instruments.gap: No Redland City Council financial assistance grant figure is stated, and no island share of one. Council accounts were not read for this pack.

instruments.label: Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements 2018
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The arrangements themselves, activated per event, jointly funded by the Commonwealth and the state and in Queensland administered by the Queensland Reconstruction Authority.
instruments.what_it_does: Sets out the relief and recovery measures that can be funded after an eligible disaster and how the Commonwealth and the state share the cost. Replaced the Natural Disaster Relief and Recovery Arrangements on 1 November 2018.
instruments.why_it_matters: The most likely single moment the Commonwealth pays for something on this island is after a storm, and even then the money comes through a Queensland authority. A council that has just lost a foreshore does not ring Canberra.
instruments.gap: No cost-sharing percentage is stated here. The share varies by measure and by the state's expenditure against thresholds, and no figure was confirmed to this pack's standard.

instruments.label: Indigenous Rangers Program
instruments.what_it_does: A Commonwealth program administered by the National Indigenous Australians Agency that funds Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land and sea management work. The agency publishes a Quandamooka Rangers project among the land and sea management projects it funds.
instruments.why_it_matters: The lever this pack calls ranger-program-funding has always named the Australian Government among its deciders and never named the program. This is it.
instruments.gap: The NIAA project page returned 403 to this agent and was identified through search results rather than read. No funding amount, no agreement term and no ranger headcount is stated here, and nothing is asserted about how QYAC runs the work. See docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md, which holds that QYAC has not seen this project.

instruments.label: Mobile Black Spot Program
instruments.what_it_does: Co-funds new and upgraded mobile base stations in regional and remote Australia, with the Commonwealth contributing up to 50 per cent of the total solution cost and the rest coming from carriers, state governments and councils. Rounds run periodically. Round 8 was announced as 55 million dollars of Commonwealth co-funding targeted at disaster-prone locations.
instruments.why_it_matters: The statutory infrastructure provider regime guarantees a connection to a house. Nothing guarantees a bar of signal on the road where somebody has just hit a koala, and this is the only Commonwealth mechanism that addresses that, on a competitive round, against every other regional place in Australia.
instruments.gap: Whether any Minjerribah site has ever been funded under any round was not established. Nothing here says the island has been in a round or has been passed over.

instruments.label: Biosecurity Act 2015
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Chapter 4, which manages the biosecurity risk of aircraft and vessels entering Australian territory from outside it, including by determining which landing places and ports are first points of entry.
instruments.what_it_does: Holds the national border against pests and diseases arriving from outside Australia.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is recorded here mostly for what it does not do. Nothing on Minjerribah is a first point of entry, so the biosecurity a player will actually meet on this island, the weeds, the fire ants, the foxes and the marine pests moving from the mainland, is Queensland's under the Biosecurity Act 2014, not the Commonwealth's. The Commonwealth's weight is at the border and in nationally cost-shared eradication programs such as the fire ant program, which every state, every territory and the Commonwealth fund and Queensland delivers.
instruments.gap: No fire ant detection on Minjerribah is claimed here and none was looked for. The point of this record is the division of responsibility, not the pest.

instruments.label: The Convention on Wetlands (the Ramsar Convention)
instruments.parties: Australia and the other contracting parties. Adopted at Ramsar in Iran in 1971 and in force from 1975.
instruments.what_it_does: Each contracting party commits to designate suitable wetlands for the List of Wetlands of International Importance, to plan for the conservation of the listed ones and as far as possible the wise use of all its wetlands, to arrange to be informed at the earliest possible time if the ecological character of a listed wetland has changed, is changing or is likely to change through technological developments, pollution or other human interference, and to report any such change to the Convention. Wise use is defined as maintaining a wetland's ecological character.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Nothing in the Convention is an offence in Australia. What bites is section 16 of the EPBC Act, which turns the listing into a Commonwealth approval requirement, and section 335, which carries the Australian Ramsar Management Principles.
instruments.obliges: Australia, in international law. It obliges no person on this island and it forbids no act here.
instruments.why_it_matters: Australia designated the world's first Wetland of International Importance, Cobourg Peninsula, in 1974, and the site this island sits inside was listed under this Convention nineteen years later. The obligation that reaches Minjerribah most directly is the reporting one, and this twin already models a mechanism that could engage it: a roost flushed often enough that the birds using it stop being able to leave in condition.
instruments.quote: arrange to be informed at the earliest possible time if the ecological character of any listed wetland has changed, is changing or is likely to change as a result of technological developments, pollution or other human interference, and report any such changes to the Ramsar Convention
instruments.gap: The Convention text itself was not read for this pack. The commitments above are the administering department's own list of what Australia accepted, from a fact sheet it published in 2012, and no article number is stated for any of them here except 3.2, which that department names in its own words.

instruments.label: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (the Bonn Convention)
instruments.parties: Australia and the other parties. Done at Bonn on 23 June 1979. Australia's Treaty Series citation is [1991] ATS 32, dated 1 September 1991.
instruments.what_it_does: Appendix I lists migratory species that are endangered. Appendix II lists migratory species that would benefit from international agreements. For an Appendix I species, a party that is a range state shall endeavour to conserve and where feasible and appropriate restore the habitats of importance in removing the species from danger of extinction, to prevent, remove, compensate for or minimise the adverse effects of activities or obstacles that seriously impede or prevent migration, and to prevent, reduce or control the factors endangering it, and shall prohibit taking, subject to four narrow exceptions. For an Appendix II species a party shall endeavour to conclude agreements.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article III, paragraphs 4 and 5, for an Appendix I species. In Australia it bites at one remove: a bird on Appendix I or II must be placed on the migratory species list under the EPBC Act, and section 20 then applies to anybody.
instruments.obliges: Australia, in international law, and the verb in Article III(4) is endeavour. That is an obligation of effort on a government rather than a prohibition on a person, and the Convention does not say what counts as having tried.
instruments.why_it_matters: The eastern curlew on the flats off Dunwich has been on Appendix II since 1979 and on Appendix I, the endangered list, since 2011. Article III(4)(a) is about habitat, and the habitat in question here is a high tide roost you can walk onto from a caravan park.
instruments.quote: to conserve and, where feasible and appropriate, restore those habitats of the species which are of importance in removing the species from danger of extinction
instruments.gap: The date the Convention entered into force generally, and the date Australia ratified, were not confirmed from a primary source and are not stated. The Australian Treaty Series text was not read: the citation comes from the administering department's own link to it. Whether any of the other shorebirds this twin models sits on a CMS appendix was not established, so this pack names only the eastern curlew.

instruments.label: East Asian-Australasian Flyway Partnership
instruments.parties: Countries, intergovernmental agencies, international non-government organisations and the international business sector, by endorsing the partnership document. Launched 6 November 2006 as a Ramsar regional initiative.
instruments.what_it_does: Maintains a network of sites recognised as internationally important for migratory waterbirds along the flyway, from New Zealand to Alaska and Russia. Moreton Bay is on that network as site EAAF013. In Australia a site is nominated with the consent of the owner or manager and the endorsement of the state government, and the Commonwealth submits it.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Nothing. There is no offence, no approval, no plan and no duty attached to a Flyway Network Site.
instruments.obliges: Nobody, as a matter of law. Its whole force is that a number of countries have agreed to pay attention to the same list of places.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is what an international arrangement looks like with no teeth at all, and it is worth a player seeing one beside the Ramsar listing over the same water. Same bay, same birds, same sand. One of those two listings carries a Commonwealth offence and the other carries none, and telling them apart is most of what this block is for.
instruments.quote: At both national level and in Queensland, there are no legally binding implications for sites designated in the Flyway Site Network. In terms of management, owners/managers are not required to alter their existing land-use or provide any formal plans.

instruments.label: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
instruments.kind: United Nations declaration, which is not a treaty
instruments.parties: Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in September 2007. Australia was one of four countries that voted against it at the time, and the Australian Government made a statement in support of it on 3 April 2009.
instruments.what_it_does: Sets out a standard of human rights for indigenous peoples: in the Australian Human Rights Commission's description, principles of equality, non-discrimination, partnership, consultation and cooperation between indigenous peoples and governments. It creates no new rights, and elaborates existing international human rights norms as they apply to indigenous peoples.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Nothing bites. It is not a treaty, it is not legally binding, it has not been incorporated into Australian domestic law, and it cannot override Australian law.
instruments.obliges: Nobody, as a matter of law. Australia's support for it is a statement of position, which is a different kind of thing from every other instrument in this pack.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is named here because a twin of Quandamooka Country that catalogued the instruments reaching this island and left this one out would be making a choice, and because its status is easy to get wrong in both directions: it is neither binding law nor nothing. What is binding on this island is the Native Title Act 1993 and the determinations and agreements made under it, which are already in this pack and are an entirely different kind of instrument.
instruments.handling: This record describes an instrument and its status in Australian law. It states no Quandamooka or QYAC position on it, asserts nothing about what it should mean on this island, and makes no claim about native title. Whether it belongs in this project at all is a question on the queue in docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md.
instruments.quote: The Declaration is not legally binding and it does not compel governments to certain actions. Rather, it is an aspirational human rights instrument that explicitly encourages harmonious and cooperative relations between governments and Indigenous peoples.
instruments.gap: The General Assembly resolution number and the exact date of adoption were not confirmed for this pack, so only the month and year are given. Whether any Australian court or tribunal has referred to the Declaration was not researched, and this pack does not say.

instruments.label: The Paris Agreement
instruments.parties: Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Australia among them. In force from 4 November 2016.
instruments.what_it_does: Each party prepares, communicates and maintains a nationally determined contribution on emissions, and reports on it. It says nothing about a local government, a foreshore or a planning scheme.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Not this island, directly. Nothing in it reaches a council. The duty that does reach a coastal council in Queensland arrives through the state, as a required planning figure.
instruments.obliges: Australia, in international law, on emissions.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the honest shape of the climate chain and it is worth showing rather than implying. A player looking for the treaty that makes this council plan for the water coming up will not find one. What they will find is a Queensland requirement, a number, and a council strategy that adopts it, and the number is 0.8 m by 2100.
instruments.gap: The Agreement text was not read for this pack, so what it obliges is stated only at the level this pack can stand behind and no article is cited. The date Australia ratified was not confirmed and is not stated, nor is the date and place of adoption. What is stated is the date it entered into force, which the UNFCCC publishes.

instruments.label: The Queensland sea level rise planning figure
instruments.what_it_does: The Queensland Government requires coastal hazard planning to adopt a sea level rise of 0.8 m by 2100. Redland City Council's Coastal Hazard Adaptation Strategy adopts it, with 0.41 m by 2070, and maps erosion and storm tide inundation for present day, 2070 and 2100 planning horizons against a 1 per cent annual exceedance probability event.
instruments.the_part_that_bites: It is the number every coastal hazard line on this island is drawn to, the declared erosion prone area included.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the rung where climate policy stops being a treaty and becomes a line on a map at Amity Point. The council's own strategy gives Amity Point an adaptation response of Mitigate, while Point Lookout is monitor, maintain and prepare, and Dunwich is monitor, maintain and prepare moving to Mitigate. Amity Point is the one place on this island the council has already decided it will have to act on.
instruments.quote: As required by the Queensland Government, a sea level rise of 0.8m by 2100 has been adopted for the Coastal Hazard Adaptation Strategy (with 0.41m by 2070).
instruments.gap: The Queensland instrument imposing the requirement was not identified by name: the council's strategy says the Queensland Government requires it and this record says no more than that. The adaptation responses come from Table 5 on p. 19, whose planning horizon columns could not be resolved from the extracted text, so no year is attached to any of them here.

national_environmental_significance.about: The matters of national environmental significance this island actually carries, each named against the EPBC Act section that protects it and against the record in data/ecology.json the twin already simulates. This block is the join. It does not create a lever and it does not decide anything: it says what a proponent has to think about before doing something here, and what a player is looking at when the shorebird readout moves.
national_environmental_significance.handling: A matter listed here is a fact about Commonwealth law and about the ecology pack. It is not a claim that any particular lever needs a referral. Whether a specific action is likely to have a significant impact is a judgement for the proponent and then for the minister, and this project does not make it.

matters.here: The Moreton Bay Ramsar site, listed 22 October 1993, takes in North Stradbroke Island. Over 120,000 hectares bay-wide.

The eastern curlew and the bar-tailed godwit on the western sand flats, both on the annexes to the three bilateral migratory bird agreements. Moreton Bay is recorded as supporting some 28 species of migratory shorebirds and over 30,000 individuals in summer.
matters.note: The shorebird system already models a roost flush costing a bird fuel it has to make back before it can fly north. Nothing in the civic layer knew that was a Commonwealth matter.

matters.matter: Listed threatened species and ecological communities
matters.here: The eastern curlew is Critically Endangered. The bar-tailed godwit is listed by subspecies rather than as a species, and the one data/ecology.json carries for these flats is the western Alaskan Limosa lapponica baueri at Endangered. The koala, in the combined Queensland, New South Wales and Australian Capital Territory populations, was listed as Endangered on 12 February 2022, which is the koala this island's habitat overlay argues about. The endangered swamp daisy Olearia hygrophila is published as found only on North Stradbroke Island.
matters.gap: The swamp daisy is not in data/ecology.json. It came out of a Queensland Wetlands Program fact sheet during this pass and has not been researched as a species record. Somebody should add it.
matters.precision_note: An earlier version of this record said the bar-tailed godwit was Endangered, full stop, which is less precise than the ecology pack it cites: that pack names the subspecies. This record does not state a status for any other subspecies of Limosa lapponica, because none was read for this pack.

matters.epbc_section: section 23, with the whale offences at Part 13 Division 3
matters.here: The water beyond three nautical miles from the territorial sea baseline off the ocean coast, which is where the Australian Whale Sanctuary begins.

not_here.why: There is none on or around this island.

not_here.matter: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park
not_here.why: It begins far to the north of Moreton Bay.

not_here.matter: Water resources from coal seam gas or a large coal mine
not_here.why: The island's mining was mineral sand and it ended in 2019. This trigger is specific to coal and coal seam gas and does not reach sand.
not_here.note: Worth stating plainly, because the island's aquifer is the thing most people would expect national water law to protect and it is not what that trigger is for.

treaty_layer.about: Seven instruments that sit above every lever on this board, and one state requirement that shows where an eighth actually lands. None of them is a decision anybody here gets to make, none of them changes when a council does, and none of them can be persuaded, funded, delayed or voted out. They are in this pack because the twin already simulates the thing four of them are about: migratory shorebirds on the western sand flats, spending on a flushed roost the fat they need to reach the northern hemisphere.
treaty_layer.not_a_tier: These are deliberately not in jurisdiction.tiers. A tier in this pack is an order of authority that decides something on this island, and none of these decides anything. Australia carries them. Nobody at that level sits in a room here, holds a lever, answers a submission or stands for election, and modelling them as a tier would invite a player to try to persuade one, which is exactly the wrong lesson.
treaty_layer.not_a_lever: An obligation is not a lever and must never be given one. Nothing in this block can be enacted, ceased, funded or stepped up, and src/systems/civic/policy.js gives it no path into a magnitude. What a player can change is the state of the world an obligation reads. The only things that move in here are whether an obligation is engaged, whether it is at issue, and how many days it has been at issue for, and that last number does not reset when anything else does.
treaty_layer.not_a_veto: The single most important thing in this block is that an international agreement is almost never a prohibition. Read the force field before reading anything else. One of the nine obligations below prohibits an act, and the act it prohibits does not occur in this simulation. Four of them oblige a government to try. One obliges a government to write something down. One requires an approval, and that one is a domestic statute rather than a treaty. Two have no legal force at all. Building this layer as a veto would have been as wrong as leaving it out, and it would have been a great deal more satisfying, which is how you can tell.

force_scale.prohibits: The instrument forbids an act outright.
force_scale.requires_approval: An act may not be taken without somebody's approval, and the approval is refusable.
force_scale.requires_report: Somebody has to tell somebody else that a thing has happened. Nothing is forbidden and nothing is refused.
force_scale.requires_effort: A government is obliged to try, in the instrument's own words, and the instrument does not say what counts as having tried hard enough.
force_scale.shapes: No legal force at all. It changes what people attend to, and nothing else.

treaty_layer.the_chain: Read the block in this order and it makes one sentence. A bird is listed on the annex to a treaty with Japan, China or the Republic of Korea, or on an appendix to the Bonn Convention. Because it is listed there, Australian law must put it on the EPBC migratory species list. Because it is on that list, section 20 applies to any person taking an action likely to have a significant impact on it. And the bird is standing on a sand flat off Dunwich, in a wetland listed under a fourth treaty, in a country whose only obligation under that one is to notice if the place changes and say so. Four instruments, three of which forbid nothing, and one Australian statute at the end that is the only rung anybody on this island ever touches.
treaty_layer.handling: Every obligation here is a description of a published instrument, and every one carries what it does not do beside what it does. No obligation is a claim that any lever on this board needs a referral, an approval or a notification. Whether a particular action is likely to have a significant impact is a judgement for a proponent and then for a minister, and this project does not make it, which is the same stop src/systems/civic/council.js already takes and for the same reason.
treaty_layer.reading_the_triggers: engaged_when and at_issue_when are read by src/systems/civic/policy.js and the vocabulary is deliberately tiny: always, never, or a published read model field tested above or below a number. A trigger that names a system the twin has not built reports itself as not connected and contributes nothing, which is the same discipline the live couplings in that file already keep.

obligations.obliges: Australia plans for the conservation of its listed wetlands and, as far as possible, the wise use of all of them. Wise use is defined as maintaining a wetland's ecological character.
obligations.binds: The Commonwealth of Australia, in international law.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody on this island. No resident, business, council officer or ranger is under this obligation.
obligations.domestic_route: The EPBC Act carries it as the Australian Ramsar Management Principles, section 335, and as a duty on the Commonwealth to use its best endeavours to see that a management plan is in place for a Ramsar site in state land and waters.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It does not forbid anything, it does not stop a development, and there is no number at which it is breached. As far as possible is the whole of the standard.

engaged_when.says: The island is inside the site. This one is engaged on every day of the game and cannot be switched off.

obligations.obliges: Australia arranges to be informed at the earliest possible time if the ecological character of a listed wetland has changed, is changing or is likely to change through technological developments, pollution or other human interference, and notifies the Ramsar Secretariat. Notification is required only for human-induced adverse change, and it is about character rather than about the criteria the site was listed for: a site can change character without ceasing to be internationally important.
obligations.binds: The Commonwealth of Australia, through its Administrative Authority, which makes the final decision on whether to notify.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody, and this is the one obligation in the block with a doorway for an ordinary person in it. The department's own account of the process says an initial assessment may begin because site managers, the site owner, a reporting mechanism or a third party told it something. A resident who counts birds is a third party.
