obligations.domestic_route: An assessment made in collaboration with the site owners and managers, against national guidance, followed by a decision that rests with the Administrative Authority alone.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It refuses nothing and forbids nothing. Nobody is fined and no project stops. What happens is that Australia has to write it down, in public, and say what is being done about it.

engaged_when.says: Engaged for as long as the site is listed.

at_issue_when.says: The twin's own shorebird indicator has fallen below the band it set for itself, and the fall is human-induced in the model: it comes from roost flushing, which is dogs, drones, vehicles and people.

obligations.modelling_note: The indicator is this simulation's own and it is not an ecological character assessment. A real one is made against the site's ecological character description, on evidence, by Australian governments together, and this twin does not make it and does not pretend to. What the indicator does is tell a player when the island they are running has reached the kind of state that would put the question on somebody's desk.

obligations.obliges: A party that is a range state of an Appendix I species shall endeavour to conserve and, where feasible and appropriate, restore the habitats of importance in removing the species from danger of extinction; to prevent, remove, compensate for or minimise the adverse effects of activities or obstacles that seriously impede or prevent migration; and to prevent, reduce or control the factors endangering it.
obligations.binds: The Commonwealth of Australia, as a range state. The verb is endeavour.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody directly. A high tide roost on the western flats is habitat of importance within the meaning of the Article, and no one standing on it is under a duty from this instrument.
obligations.domestic_route: An Appendix I or Appendix II bird must be placed on the migratory species list under the EPBC Act, which is what makes section 20 apply to it.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It does not make disturbance an offence, and endeavour has no threshold in it. A country that is trying and failing is not in breach of Article III(4).

engaged_when.says: Engaged whenever an Appendix I bird is on the island. The eastern curlew is here from about August to March, and a few immatures over-winter, so this one comes and goes with the season.

obligations.obliges: A party that is a range state of an Appendix I species shall prohibit the taking of animals of that species. Exceptions may be made only for scientific purposes, to enhance the propagation or survival of the species, to accommodate the needs of traditional subsistence users, or where extraordinary circumstances require, and any exception must be precise as to content and limited in space and time.
obligations.binds: Australia, which must enact the prohibition, and through Australian law, any person.
obligations.binds_here: Anybody on this island, in the sense that killing or capturing an eastern curlew is not something a permit from the council would ever cover.
obligations.domestic_route: The offence provisions of the EPBC Act and Queensland's Nature Conservation Act 1992.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: Taking means killing, injuring or capturing. It is not disturbance. Flushing a roost is not taking, this twin does not model taking at all, and the one obligation in this block that genuinely prohibits something prohibits a thing that does not happen in this simulation. That is worth knowing rather than hiding: the instrument with the sharpest teeth is the one least engaged by anything a player does.

engaged_when.says: Nothing in this simulation takes a bird. No lever, no event and no agent can.

obligations.article: The three bilateral agreements, taken together
obligations.obliges: Protection and conservation of migratory birds and their important habitats, protection from take or trade except in limited circumstances, the exchange of information, and building cooperative relationships. The parties meet in consultation every two years and Australia files a national report.
obligations.binds: Australia, and Japan, the People's Republic of China and the Republic of Korea in their own territories.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody. Their real weight on this island is upstream of anything anybody does here: a bird on one of the three annexes must go on the EPBC migratory species list, and that listing is what section 20 hangs on.
obligations.domestic_route: Annex to migratory species list to EPBC Act section 20.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: None of the three forbids disturbing a roost, and none of them can be enforced by anybody on this island against anybody else. What they do is make a bird on a sand flat off Dunwich a subject of four countries' foreign policy, which is a different kind of protection and a real one.
obligations.the_other_end: The pressure these agreements exist to meet is mostly not here. The flyway decline the shorebird model carries is driven by habitat loss on the staging grounds, above all the Yellow Sea, and that is beyond any island lever. These three treaties are the only mechanism in this pack through which that is anybody's business at all.

engaged_when.says: Engaged whenever annex-listed birds are on the island.

obligations.article: Part 3: section 16 for a Ramsar wetland, section 18 for a listed threatened species, section 20 for a listed migratory species
obligations.obliges: A person must not take an action that has, will have or is likely to have a significant impact on a matter of national environmental significance without the environment minister's approval.
obligations.binds: Any person. This is the only rung of the whole chain that reaches somebody standing on the sand.
obligations.binds_here: Anybody proposing an action on this island that would significantly affect the Ramsar wetland, the listed migratory birds on it, or the listed threatened species.
obligations.domestic_route: It is the domestic route. It is where the four instruments above stop being foreign policy and become a form somebody has to lodge.
obligations.the_distinction_that_matters: Section 16 is about a place and section 20 is about a bird, and they do not have the same footprint. The Ramsar line steps around the three townships; the migratory species listing does not step around anything. An action outside the site that is likely to significantly affect a listed migratory bird engages section 20 just the same, because the section is about the species and not about a boundary. That is why the exclusion areas on this island are less of a relief than they look.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It does not decide anything in advance and it is not a veto. Whether a particular action is likely to have a significant impact is a judgement for the proponent and then for the minister. This project does not make that judgement, this obligation record does not make it, and nothing here says any lever on this board needs a referral.

engaged_when.says: The matters are here, so the Act reaches this ground on every day of the game.

obligations.obliges: Nothing enforceable. Owners and managers of a Flyway Network Site are encouraged to protect the waterbirds it was listed for, and their habitats, by voluntarily applying wise use principles.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody, and it is worth saying plainly rather than letting a listing imply a duty. Moreton Bay is site EAAF013 and no owner or manager has to alter a land use or produce a plan because of it.
obligations.domestic_route: None. There is no Australian statute behind it.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: Everything. This is the control in the experiment: an international listing over the same water as the Ramsar one, with none of its force. If a player learns to tell the two apart, this block has done its job.

engaged_when.says: The listing stands whatever anybody does. So does its lack of consequence.

obligations.obliges: Nothing, as a matter of law. It is not a treaty, it is not binding, and it has not been incorporated into Australian domestic law.
obligations.binds_here: Nobody. Australia's support for it, stated on 3 April 2009, is a position rather than an instrument.
obligations.domestic_route: None. The instruments that do bind on this island in this area are the Native Title Act 1993, the 2011 determinations made under it and the two registered indigenous land use agreements, all of which are already in this pack.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It cannot override Australian law and it creates no new rights. It is listed here because leaving it out of a catalogue of instruments would itself be a statement, and because getting its status wrong in either direction is easy.

engaged_when.says: Nothing in this simulation engages it, and no lever, metric or event in this pack is joined to it.

obligations.handling: This record describes the instrument's legal status and nothing else. It states no Quandamooka or QYAC position, models nothing, and derives nothing. Whether it belongs in this project at all is on the queue in docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md, and the answer is not this pack's to give.

obligations.obliges: Coastal hazard planning adopts a sea level rise of 0.8 m by 2100. The council's Coastal Hazard Adaptation Strategy adopts it, with 0.41 m by 2070.
obligations.binds: Redland City Council, through the state.
obligations.binds_here: The council, and through its maps, anybody who wants to build near the line.
obligations.domestic_route: Queensland to the council to the strategy to a hazard map to the erosion prone area already in this pack.
obligations.what_it_does_not_do: It does not come from the Paris Agreement, and the honest finding of this whole block is that the climate treaty reaches this island through nothing. It reaches Canberra. What reaches Amity Point is a state requirement and a number.

engaged_when.says: The figure is in force whether or not anybody on the board is thinking about it. Amity Point is the one island locality the council has already assigned an adaptation response of Mitigate.

commonwealth_money.about: How Commonwealth money reaches Minjerribah, and the honest shape of it, which is the thing a player should learn from this tier.
commonwealth_money.the_honest_note: Most federal money that lands on this island does not arrive from the Commonwealth. It arrives through Queensland, or through Redland City Council, having been paid to one of them first. By the time it is spent on a footpath or a ranger's wage, nothing about it is labelled federal. That is why a player who goes looking for a Commonwealth lever finds almost none, and it is not because the Commonwealth is not paying.

routes.reaches_the_island_via: The Queensland Reconstruction Authority, jointly funded with the state, activated per event
A National Indigenous Australians Agency program, direct to the funded organisation
routes.note: One of the few routes with no state or council in the middle of it.

routes.reaches_the_island_via: A competitive Commonwealth round, co-funded by carriers, the state and the council

commonwealth_money.gap: No dollar figure for any Commonwealth payment touching Minjerribah was established. This block describes routes, not amounts, and it should not be read as saying the Commonwealth spends much or little here.

off_world.about: The off-world register. Two things kept apart on purpose: the law that already reaches above the nation state and binds Australia, which is cited like anything else in this pack; and, marked separately at every point of contact, the shape an instrument would have to take if this island ever answered to an authority above the nation state. Nothing in this block is part of the island's default state. No lever cites it, no metric moves with it, no purse touches it, and the interface leaves it switched off until somebody asks for it.
off_world.why_it_is_here: docs/DIRECTION.md item 6 settles the method: claims wear labels, known, modelled or speculative; the three registers stay visually distinct everywhere; and speculative material never blends into the default island state. Everything else in this file is a known claim with a citation behind it. This block is the one place the twin can hold a genuinely forward claim beside a statute without either one contaminating the other, and it is the only block in the file allowed to describe something that does not exist.
off_world.the_question: The treaty layer in this pack answers a real question for a bird. An eastern curlew on the western sand flats is covered by three bilateral agreements and a wetland listing, so an obligation made above the Australian state reaches down to a mudflat on this island and binds what may be done to it. This register asks the same question one tier up, and it is not an idle one: if this island ever had to answer to an authority above the nation state, what would the instrument be, who would hold it, and what would it oblige. Two working answers already exist, over Antarctica and over the deep seabed, and Australia is a party to both.
off_world.why_off_by_default: A councillor should be able to open the civic board, work through every lever in it and never learn this block exists, without losing anything. Speculative material that arrives unasked is the thing that makes a person stop trusting the sourced material next to it. So it is a switch, it starts off, it can be switched back off, and while it is off nothing anywhere in this build differs by so much as a number.

registers.known: A sourced fact: a treaty in force, a statute, a published policy, a recorded event. Every record here carries its citation and its confidence on the same scale as the rest of the pack.
registers.modelled: This pack's own reading of two or more known records, stated as a reading and never as a fact, with the test that would settle or move it named on the record.
registers.speculative: An instrument that does not exist. Every one is modelled on a named real instrument, held by an office that is named as invented, and carries the test that would settle it. Nothing here is a forecast, a proposal to anybody, or advice.

rules: Off by default. It is turned on deliberately and can be turned off again.

It changes no number in the default island state: not a budget, not a sentiment, not a lever's outcome. The one-way rule is executable: this block may name a lever, and no lever, metric, issue or institution in this pack may name anything in this block. tools/ingest/checks-offworld.mjs fails the gate if that direction ever reverses.
It is visually distinct from the first pixel. Every speculative record wears its marker wherever it is drawn, not only in a header.

No speculative instrument is ever attributed to a real body. The Australian Space Agency is not given a power it does not have, and neither is anybody else. Invented offices are named as invented and hold nothing.
Nothing cultural, ever. The prohibitions in data/lore.json bind this register exactly as they bind the rest of the file, and an off-world frame is not a way around them.

Every record cites. A treaty gets its name, its year, its parties and what it obliges. A statute gets its short title and the part that bites. A speculative instrument gets the real one it was lifted from.
off_world.cultural_gate: This block asserts nothing about Quandamooka law, knowledge, position or interest, and infers nothing. Where the obvious speculative move would touch any of that, the record says so and stops: see not_here below. QYAC has not seen this project, and docs/CULTURAL-REVIEW.md holds the first question, which stands over this block as it stands over everything else.
off_world.not_advice: Nothing in this block is legal advice, financial advice or a proposal to anybody. Where a record describes a payment, a fund or a claim, it is proposed, not offered: nothing in this repository operates any of them.

instruments.label: Outer Space Treaty 1967
instruments.full_title: Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article II, the non-appropriation principle. Article VI, which makes a state internationally responsible for national activities in outer space, including those carried on by its non-governmental entities, and requires that those be authorised and continuously supervised by the state. Article VII, the liability of a launching state. Article IX, the duty to avoid harmful contamination of celestial bodies and adverse changes in the environment of the Earth.
instruments.what_it_does: Sets the constitutional frame for everything anybody does off world: exploration and use for the benefit of all countries, free access, no national appropriation, no weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on celestial bodies, state responsibility for private actors, and liability for damage.
instruments.quote: Outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.
instruments.australia: [1967] ATS 24. Australia's instrument of ratification was deposited on 10 October 1967, the day the treaty entered into force.
instruments.why_it_matters: Article VI is the one that would reach an island. If anybody here ever operated anything off world it would not be their activity in the eyes of international law; it would be Australia's, and Australia would have to authorise it and keep supervising it. There is no council-shaped hole in that sentence, which is the same finding this pack keeps making at every other tier.

instruments.label: Rescue Agreement 1968
instruments.full_title: Agreement on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space
instruments.the_part_that_bites: A state that learns of a space object having returned to territory under its jurisdiction notifies the launching authority and the United Nations Secretary-General, and, on request and with assistance from the launching authority, recovers and returns it.
instruments.what_it_does: Elaborates the rescue and return duties in Article V and Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty: assistance to personnel in distress, and the return of objects that come down where they were not meant to.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the treaty that would decide what happened next if a piece of somebody's spacecraft came down on this island. Not the council, and not the finder.
instruments.australia: Australia is a party. The Australian Space Agency lists it among the five United Nations space treaties Australia is party to.

instruments.label: Liability Convention 1972
instruments.full_title: Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article II: a launching state is absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight. Absolute means no fault has to be shown. Article VIII: the claim is presented by a state, through diplomatic channels.
instruments.what_it_does: Sets who pays when something falls, and who may ask.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the closest off-world law comes to a street on this island, and the shape of it is this twin's own subject. If a piece of a re-entering space object landed on a roof in Dunwich the liability would be absolute, and the person under the roof could not bring the claim. A state presents it. The remedy runs upward through the Commonwealth, exactly as an environmental referral does, and a council has no verb in it at all.
instruments.gap: Whether Australia has ever presented a claim under it was not established for this pack. No such claim was found.

instruments.label: Registration Convention 1975
instruments.full_title: Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space
instruments.the_part_that_bites: A launching state maintains a register of the objects it launches and furnishes the United Nations Secretary-General with the information about each of them.
instruments.what_it_does: Makes the population of orbit a matter of public record rather than a matter anybody has to guess at.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the only one of the five that is mostly an administrative duty, and it is the reason the speculative register below can be specific about what a registrar does: there is a real one to copy.
instruments.australia: Australia is a party and maintains a national register.

instruments.label: Moon Agreement 1979
instruments.full_title: Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article 11, which declares the Moon and its natural resources the common heritage of mankind and undertakes an international regime to govern their exploitation.
instruments.what_it_does: Takes the Outer Space Treaty's non-appropriation principle further than any other space instrument in force: not only may no state appropriate the Moon, but its resources are common heritage, and the parties commit to build a regime over their exploitation once that becomes feasible.
instruments.quote: States Parties to this Agreement hereby undertake to establish an international regime, including appropriate procedures, to govern the exploitation of the natural resources of the moon as such exploitation is about to become feasible.
instruments.australia: Australia acceded, rather than signed and ratified, and the instrument was lodged in 1986. [1986] ATS 14. The Lowy Institute's account of the archival record puts the accession in the Hawke government's disarmament and arms control commitments of that year.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the genuinely interesting fact about Australia's position, and it is why the off-world register is worth having at all rather than being whimsy. Australia is one of a very small number of states bound by a common heritage rule over off-world resources. Most spacefaring states are not parties: the United States, Russia and China have not ratified it, and France and India signed without ratifying. That was a curiosity until 2020, when Australia became a founding signatory of a set of principles that take a different practical line on the same question. Both are current.
instruments.gap: The number of states parties moves and this record does not state one. UNOOSA publishes the status table annually and that is where the current number lives.

instruments.label: The Artemis Accords
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The section headed Space Resources, which records the signatories' view that the extraction and use of space resources can be done in a manner that complies with the Outer Space Treaty, and the section headed Deconfliction of Space Activities, which introduces notified safety zones around an operation. Neither is a treaty obligation. The Accords are political commitments and say so.
instruments.what_it_does: Sets a common set of principles among the states operating in the Artemis program: peaceful purposes, transparency, interoperability, emergency assistance, registration, release of scientific data, protection of outer space heritage, space resources, deconfliction and orbital debris.
instruments.australia: Australia was one of the eight founding signatories on 13 October 2020, with Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. The list has grown well past fifty since; NASA publishes the current count and this record does not restate it.
instruments.why_it_matters: Australia is a party to the Moon Agreement and a founding signatory of the Accords, and the two take different practical lines on the same question. That is not this project's observation: it is reported by a named Australian institute and cited here as such.
instruments.gap: The section numbering was not read from the signed text, so this record names the sections by their headings rather than by number. A section number nobody checked is worse than no section number, because a reader has no way to tell.

instruments.label: Space (Launches and Returns) Act 2018
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The permit regime. A launch from Australia, a return to Australia, an Australian launching a payload overseas, and a high power rocket, each need an authorisation, and a launch permit carries an insurance or financial responsibility requirement running to a hundred million dollars.
instruments.what_it_does: Is the domestic half of the treaties above. It is the amended Space Activities Act 1998, renamed in 2018, and it is how Australia discharges the Outer Space Treaty's Article VI duty to authorise and continuously supervise, and the Registration Convention's duty to keep a register.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the answer to a question the treaties alone do not settle, and one docs/SOURCES.md already teaches from the owner's own 2012 treaty stack: being a party to a treaty and having it operate in Australian domestic law are not the same thing, and the second needs legislation. This is that legislation.

instruments.label: The COSPAR Planetary Protection Policy
instruments.kind: a scientific body's policy, not law
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Mission categories, running from a target of no interest for contamination up to a return of unsterilised material to Earth, with the handling requirements rising with the category.
instruments.what_it_does: Gives practical effect to Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which requires states to avoid harmful contamination of celestial bodies and adverse changes in the Earth's environment from returned matter. Space agencies adopt it and design missions to it.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the best existing answer to the question this register asks, and it is not a law. COSPAR is a committee of scientists with no power to compel anybody. Its policy binds agencies because they adopt it, and because a mission that ignored it would not find partners. An authority above the nation state that holds no legal power and is obeyed anyway already exists, which is worth knowing before imagining one that holds power.
instruments.gap: The current category definitions were not read line by line for this pack, so this record describes the shape of the policy and states no category's requirements.

instruments.label: Radiocommunications Act 1992
instruments.the_part_that_bites: The apparatus licence. An earth station on the ground that talks to a space station needs a licence from the Australian Communications and Media Authority: an earth licence for the uplink, an earth receive licence for the downlink.
instruments.what_it_does: Licenses the use of the radiofrequency spectrum in Australia, including every dish pointed at a satellite.
instruments.why_it_matters: This is the entire footprint of off-world law on Minjerribah today, and stating it plainly is the point. A dish here that talked to a satellite would need a Commonwealth licence. That is all. No lever in this pack needs one and none is proposed, and the modelled reading below keeps that count honest rather than asserting it.

instruments.label: The Australian Radio Quiet Zone Western Australia
instruments.the_part_that_bites: An inner zone of seventy kilometres radius around the Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory in which other radiocommunications services are taken to be secondary to radio astronomy, with further constraints out to a wider zone.
instruments.what_it_does: Protects the radio telescopes at Boolardy from interference by constraining what may transmit near them, under the Radiocommunications Act 1992.
instruments.why_it_matters: It is the nearest thing in Australian law to a place-based obligation owed to the sky, and it is the reason the first speculative proposal below is a variation on a real Australian instrument rather than an invention. A Commonwealth regulator drew a line around a place so that something off world could be heard, and the people inside the line live with it.

instruments.label: The Antarctic Treaty 1959
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article I, Antarctica used for peaceful purposes only. Article IV, which freezes territorial claims: nothing done while the treaty is in force is a renunciation of a claim, a basis for one, or a recognition of anybody else's.
instruments.what_it_does: Governs a continent through a treaty and its consultative meetings rather than through any single parliament, with no sovereign in the ordinary sense.
instruments.australia: Australia is an original signatory and claims a large sector of the continent, a claim Article IV neither recognises nor renounces.
instruments.why_it_matters: The first of the two working answers to this register's question. An instrument above the nation state, over a place, that has held for more than sixty years, and the mechanism that made it hold was not deciding the hardest question but agreeing to leave it undecided.

instruments.label: The Madrid Protocol 1991
instruments.full_title: Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article 7. The prohibition cannot be removed or amended unless a binding legal regime on Antarctic mineral resource activities is in force, and for the first fifty years from entry into force the Protocol can be modified only by unanimous agreement of the Consultative Parties.
instruments.what_it_does: Designates Antarctica a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, and prohibits mining there.
instruments.quote: Any activity relating to mineral resources, other than scientific research, shall be prohibited.
instruments.australia: Australia is a party and implements it through the Antarctic Treaty (Environment Protection) Act 1980.
instruments.why_it_matters: Worth reading beside this island's own history rather than as an exotic case. Mining ended on Minjerribah at the end of 2019 under a Queensland Act. Mining is prohibited in Antarctica by a protocol to a treaty that no single parliament can repeal. Two extraction bans over two places, one made by a parliament a hundred kilometres away and one made by an instrument above every parliament. Which kind of ban a place would rather have is exactly the argument this register exists to let somebody have, and neither answer is obvious.

instruments.label: UNCLOS Part XI and the International Seabed Authority
instruments.kind: multilateral treaty and the body it created
instruments.the_part_that_bites: Article 136, which declares the Area, meaning the seabed beyond national jurisdiction, and its resources the common heritage of mankind. Part XI then creates an authority to administer them, with an assembly, a council and a secretariat, and the power to grant or withhold contracts.
instruments.what_it_does: Puts a part of the planet outside every state's jurisdiction and gives a standing international body the say over what happens to it.
instruments.quote: The Area and its resources are the common heritage of mankind.
instruments.australia: Australia is a party to the Convention and a member of the Authority.
instruments.why_it_matters: The second working answer, and the one closer to home, because it is about the seabed and this island is surrounded by water. It is also the answer that shows what such an authority costs to have: the Authority has existed since 1994, has never approved commercial exploitation, and its exploitation regulations have been under negotiation for years. An authority above the state is not a body that moves quickly, and a register that imagined one without saying so would be selling something.
instruments.gap: The Authority's current instruments and the state of the exploitation regulations were not read for this pack. This record describes the shape of the body and states nothing about any application before it.

precedents.label: Cosmos 954, and the only claim ever made
precedents.what_happened: A Soviet satellite carrying a nuclear reactor re-entered over Canada in January 1978 and scattered radioactive debris across the Northwest Territories. Canada presented a claim under the Liability Convention, and a settlement was concluded in Moscow on 2 April 1981 for three million Canadian dollars, without any express acknowledgement of legal liability.
precedents.what_it_shows: The Liability Convention has been used once in its history, state to state, and the payment was framed as a settlement rather than as liability admitted. That is the whole operating record of the instrument that would apply if something fell here.

precedents.label: The Shire of Esperance fines a space agency
precedents.what_happened: Debris from the re-entering Skylab space station came down across a stretch of Western Australia, and the Shire of Esperance issued NASA a four hundred dollar infringement for littering. Everybody involved understood it as a joke. It went unpaid for thirty years and was settled in 2009 by an American radio audience, which is not a legal remedy either.
precedents.what_it_shows: The best teaching object in this register, and it is Australian local government, which is the seat this twin puts a player in. A council met an off-world actor and found it had no instrument: not the wrong instrument, none. Under the Liability Convention the claim would have belonged to Australia, and Australia did not make one. The joke was funny because it was accurate.
precedents.gap: The 2009 payment is reported by secondary sources rather than by the shire, and the exact figure and its currency were reported as Australian dollars at the time. Nothing here turns on the amount.

readings.label: Australia holds two commitments that pull against each other
readings.reading: On off-world resources Australia is bound by a common heritage rule under the Moon Agreement and has committed politically to a position on extraction under the Artemis Accords. Both are current. The tension between them is reported by a named Australian institute, and this pack carries it as a reported tension rather than asserting a legal conclusion of its own.
readings.settling_test: A published Australian government statement reconciling the two, or a decision by an Australian regulator on an application involving space resources. Neither was found in anything read for this pack.
readings.why_it_belongs_here: It is the strongest argument in the register for taking the register seriously. A state can be a party to two instruments that answer the same question differently, hold both for years, and never be made to choose. That is worth a player knowing before they read the speculative half, because it is the ordinary condition of law above the state rather than an aberration.

readings.label: Off-world law touches this island at one point
readings.reading: Everything in the known half of this register binds Australia, and almost none of it reaches Minjerribah. The one point of contact today is an apparatus licence for a dish that talks to a satellite. That is counted rather than asserted: no lever, metric, issue or institution in this pack names anything in this block, and the check in tools/ingest/checks-offworld.mjs fails the gate if one ever does.
readings.settling_test: A proposal for a ground station, an observatory or a launch site anywhere on the island would change the count, and the first gate run after it would say so.

readings.label: A remedy from above the state runs upward, not down
readings.reading: On the operating record, a person under the roof has no standing. The Liability Convention gives the claim to a state; the one time it was used, a state brought it and a state settled it; and the one time an Australian local government tried to act on its own account the attempt had no force and everybody knew it. So the shape of an off-world remedy today is the same shape this pack finds at every other tier: the island asks, somebody else decides.
readings.settling_test: An Australian claim under the Liability Convention, of which none was found, or any instrument anywhere giving a person standing to claim directly. The speculative proposal below headed a claim a person can bring is what the second would have to look like.

readings.label: An authority above the state is slow by construction
readings.reading: Both working examples took decades to build and neither decides quickly, and in both the slowness is doing work rather than being a fault. Antarctica held because the hardest question was left undecided in Article IV. The seabed authority has existed since 1994 and has approved no commercial exploitation. Anybody imagining an instrument above the nation state for this island should price that in: the plausible version arrives slowly and refuses often.
readings.settling_test: The Authority adopting exploitation regulations, or a Consultative Meeting moving the Antarctic mining prohibition, would each be a real datum on how fast such a body can move. Until one happens the reading rests on two cases.

holders.not_given_anything_here: No instrument in the speculative half of this register is held by this body, proposed to it, or implied to be within its power.

holders.not_given_anything_here: No instrument in the speculative half of this register is held by this body, proposed to it, or implied to be within its power.

holders.label: A registrar above the state
holders.kind: an office that does not exist
holders.what_it_would_hold: A register of obligations owed to places rather than to states, and the power to publish whether an obligation was met. Nothing more: it cannot fine, licence or refuse.
holders.why_this_shape: Modelled on the Registration Convention, whose whole power is that the information is on the record. An invented office with a publishing power is the smallest one worth imagining, and the smallest one is the honest place to start.
holders.confidence_is_about: the real instrument this office is modelled on. The office itself does not exist and no confidence rating could apply to it.

holders.label: A common heritage trustee
holders.kind: an office that does not exist
holders.what_it_would_hold: A corpus of receipts from off-world resource use, and a published rule for distributing them, with no power over anybody's activities.
holders.why_this_shape: Modelled on the common heritage provisions of the Moon Agreement and Part XI of the Convention, both of which contemplate benefits shared beyond the state that did the work.
holders.confidence_is_about: the real instruments this office is modelled on. The office itself does not exist.

holders.label: A claims forum open to a person
holders.kind: an office that does not exist
holders.what_it_would_hold: Standing for a person or a household to bring a claim for off-world damage, and a fund of first resort so that a remedy does not wait on a settlement between states.
holders.why_this_shape: Modelled on the Liability Convention, and specifically on the thing that convention does not do: Article VIII gives the claim to a state.
holders.confidence_is_about: the real instrument this office is modelled on, and the fact that it gives the claim to a state. The forum itself does not exist.

holders.label: An assembly with a seat for a place
holders.kind: an office that does not exist
holders.what_it_would_hold: A hearing before a decision above the state lands on a place, and a record of what was heard. Not a vote and not a veto.
holders.why_this_shape: Modelled on the assembly of the seabed authority and on the Antarctic consultative meetings, both of which seat states and neither of which seats a place. The invented part is exactly one change to a real design.
holders.confidence_is_about: the two real bodies this office is modelled on and the fact that neither seats a sub-national place. The assembly itself does not exist.

proposals.label: A place-based obligation owed to the sky
proposals.what_it_would_be: An instrument that draws a line around a place and constrains what may be emitted from it upward: light on the seaward side, and a spectrum floor, both stated as measurements a place can take itself.
proposals.what_it_would_oblige: The place publishes its own measurements. The registrar publishes whether the obligation was met. Nobody is fined, licensed or refused, and the sanction is that the record is public.
proposals.why_this_one: Because a real Australian regulator has already done the domestic version. The Australian Radio Quiet Zone constrains what a place may transmit so that something off world can be heard, and this is that instrument one tier up, with the addition that the place holds the measurement rather than being measured.
proposals.settling_test: Whether any instrument above the nation state has ever imposed an obligation on a sub-national place directly, rather than on the state that contains it. Nothing read for this pack found one, which is the interesting part.
proposals.already_true_here: It would land on the lever this board already carries for filling in the mobile black spots, and it would land against it. That lever wants more transmission on this island and a quiet obligation wants less, so the two would have to be settled against each other by somebody. Naming the collision is the whole of the connection: the register does not move that lever, fund it or change its outcome.
proposals.the_half_with_nowhere_to_land: The light half has no lever on this board at all. The island has reasons to care about light at night that have nothing to do with astronomy, and there is no lighting lever in this pack for any of them. That gap is a finding about the pack rather than about the proposal.
proposals.confidence_is_about: the real instrument this proposal is modelled on. The proposal itself does not exist and is not before anybody.

proposals.label: A common heritage share paid to a place
proposals.what_it_would_be: An instrument under which a share of the proceeds of off-world resource use is held in trust and distributed, with places able to receive directly rather than only through the state that contains them.
proposals.what_it_would_oblige: A published allocation rule, a locked share that cannot be spent, and a patience parameter. Recipients would be real organisations, and the rule would be readable before any money moved.
proposals.why_this_one: Because the common heritage idea already exists in two instruments Australia is bound by, and in both the benefit flows to states. The single speculative change is the recipient. docs/DIRECTION.md already describes the receiving shape on the island side as a community fund with a corpus, a locked share, a published rule and a patience parameter, so the proposal is one real instrument joined to one already-written design rather than a new idea.
proposals.settling_test: Whether any benefit-sharing instrument anywhere pays a sub-national place directly. The seabed regime distributes among states parties, and this pack found no counterexample.
proposals.proposed_not_offered: Nothing in this repository operates a fund, holds money or offers a share, and none of this is financial advice.
proposals.confidence_is_about: the real instruments this proposal is modelled on. The proposal itself does not exist.

proposals.label: A claim a person can bring
proposals.what_it_would_be: Standing for a person or a household whose roof, boat or paddock is damaged by something from orbit, in a forum that does not require a government to take up their case, with a fund of first resort that pays before the states have finished arguing.
proposals.what_it_would_oblige: The launching party pays into the fund as a condition of launching. The fund pays the household on proof of damage and then recovers from the launching party in its own name.
proposals.why_this_one: Because the gap is real and documented rather than imagined. Absolute liability already exists, and the only person who cannot use it is the person it happened to. The one time an Australian local body acted on its own account, it had no instrument at all.
proposals.settling_test: Any instrument, anywhere, giving a person standing against a launching state. None was found for this pack. Insurance requirements under domestic launch law are not the same thing: they secure the launching party against a state claim, not a householder against a launching party.
proposals.already_true_here: This is the proposal that would land on nothing on this board, and that is the finding. There is no lever here for it, because there is nothing a council can do about it.
proposals.confidence_is_about: the real instrument this proposal is modelled on and the gap in it. The forum and the fund do not exist.

proposals.label: A seat for a place, not only for a state
proposals.what_it_would_be: A hearing right: before a decision made above the nation state lands on an identified place, the place is notified, heard, and the hearing is on the record. Not a vote. Not a veto.
proposals.what_it_would_oblige: Notification with time to answer, a hearing, and a written record of what was heard and what was done with it.
proposals.why_this_one: Because the generic decision shape is already in this project rather than invented for it. docs/DIRECTION.md item 8 lists a mandatory-consultation gate and an advisory chamber whose advice is recorded but not binding, drawn from published constitutional practice. This is that shape at the tier above the state, which is the one tier where it does not exist anywhere.
proposals.settling_test: Whether any body above the nation state seats a place rather than a state. Of the three examined here, the seabed authority, the Antarctic consultative meetings and the space treaty machinery, none does.
proposals.the_line_it_does_not_cross: Who the custodians of this island are, what they would want from such a seat, and whether they would want one at all, are not modelled, not inferred and not imagined here. The instrument's shape is generic; nothing in it speaks for anybody.
proposals.confidence_is_about: the real bodies this proposal is modelled on and the fact that none of them seats a place. The seat does not exist.

proposals.label: A continuity duty on an off-world service
proposals.what_it_would_be: A duty on the operator of an orbital asset that a place depends on to keep a minimum service to that place through an emergency, and to say in advance what that minimum is.
proposals.what_it_would_oblige: A published minimum, a test of it, and the result on the record. No power to compel, and no penalty beyond the record being public.
proposals.why_this_one: Because Australia already has the domestic version and this pack already cites it: the statutory infrastructure provider regime puts a service obligation on a provider. What has no equivalent is an obligation owed by an operator above the state to a place below it, and an island whose mainland link can fail is exactly where that gap is felt. docs/DIRECTION.md names the tether cut as the sharpest scenario in the economic layer, and this is the instrument that scenario would test.
proposals.settling_test: Whether any licensing regime anywhere conditions an orbital service on continuity to a named place. Australian domestic service obligations attach to carriers and to premises, not to a place's continuity through an emergency, and nothing above the state was found.
proposals.already_true_here: It would land beside the two levers on this board that are about the island holding together when the mainland stops helping: the energy resilience lever and the storm tide readiness lever. Both are about the same hour of the same bad day. The register points at them and touches neither.
proposals.confidence_is_about: the real instruments this proposal is modelled on. The duty does not exist.

never_attributed.about: Bodies that may never hold, be offered, or be implied to hold anything in the speculative half of this register. The rule is executable: tools/ingest/checks-offworld.mjs fails the gate on any speculative record whose holder resolves to a real body, and on any that names one of these in a holder or obligation field.
never_attributed.why: A speculative instrument attributed to a real body is a claim about that body, and it would be false. It is also the specific way a register like this one goes wrong: the invented part quietly borrows the credibility of a real name.
never_attributed.and_every_institution_in_this_pack: Every id in institutions[] is covered by the same rule, QYAC and Redland City Council included.

not_here.refused: An instrument that freezes claims over this island, on the Antarctic model
not_here.why: It is the obvious speculative move and this register will not make it. Native title over this island and the waters around it was determined by the Federal Court in 2011 and it is not a hypothetical for anybody to reason with, least of all a simulation. Naming the shape and stopping is the whole of what is honest here.

The prohibitions in data/lore.json bind this register exactly as they bind the rest of the file. Setting a proposal above the nation state does not make its cultural content somebody else's problem, and an off-world frame is not a route around a gate. The gate runs the same thirteen rules over this block as over every other.

not_here.refused: Defence, security and anything with an enemy in it
not_here.why: docs/DIRECTION.md records the standing constraint: no combat, no defence scenario, no enemy and no current defence event, because this twin is an argument that a place can be genuinely hard to run without anybody attacking it. A register set above the nation state is the first place a defence frame would arrive, so it is refused here by name. The owner keeps that thinking in a separate repository and none of it is imported.

not_here.refused: Dates, probabilities and anything that reads as a forecast
not_here.why: No record here says any of this will happen, should happen, or is likely. A speculative register that started predicting would have stopped being a register and become a claim.

not_here.refused: A launch site, a spaceport, a ground station or an observatory on this island
not_here.why: Nobody has proposed one. Inventing a proposal and then modelling its consequences is precisely how a plan becomes a fact by being modelled, which docs/INGEST.md names as the failure the status classifier exists to stop. If one is ever proposed it arrives as a sourced record like anything else, in the known register, not in this one.

gaps: No legal advice was taken on anything in this block and none of it is legal advice.
The number of states parties to the Moon Agreement is not stated here, because it moves and the annual UNOOSA status table is where it lives.
The Artemis Accords sections are named by heading rather than by number, because the signed text was not read line by line for this pack.

The tension between Australia's two commitments on space resources is carried as a reported tension, attributed to the institute that reported it. No Australian government statement reconciling them was found, and the absence of one is not evidence either way.
The seabed authority's current instruments and the state of its exploitation regulations were not read. Nothing here describes any application before it.
Nothing in this pack establishes whether Australia has ever presented a claim under the Liability Convention. None was found, which is not the same as none existing.
